(A) yes

I think a woman should have the ability to make that choice herself. It's a deeply personal decision that involves her own circumstances, health, and what she feels is right for her life. I don't think the government should restrict that option entirely.

I'd say **(A) yes**.

Look, I think if there's solid medical evidence showing the baby will have serious complications or defects that would cause severe suffering—especially conditions that are incompatible with life—a woman should have the option to make that choice. It's deeply personal, and I don't think the government should force someone to carry a pregnancy to term in those circumstances. That's ultimately between her, her family, and her doctors.

(A) yes

I think in cases where a woman's health is genuinely at serious risk, abortion should be a legal option. That feels like a situation where her life and wellbeing have to come first. It's a difficult circumstance, but I believe people should have access to medical care that protects their health when pregnancies become dangerous.

I'd say **(A) yes**.

Look, I think if a woman doesn't want to be pregnant—for whatever reason, whether she's married, has kids already, or whatever her situation is—that should be her decision to make. It's her body and her life. The fact that she's married doesn't really change that for me. She should have access to safe, legal abortion if that's what she decides.

(A) yes

I think if a family genuinely can't afford to support another child, that's a real hardship that matters. Forcing someone into that situation seems unfair to both the mother and any child born into those circumstances. It's a practical reality many families face, and people should have options when they're in that position.

(A) yes

I think in cases of rape, a woman should have access to legal abortion. Being forced into pregnancy against your will through violence is an extraordinary circumstance. The trauma involved and the lack of any consensual choice in the matter makes this different from other abortion scenarios in my view. A woman shouldn't be compelled to carry a pregnancy resulting from rape if she doesn't want to.

(A) yes

Look, I think it comes down to a woman having control over her own body and life decisions. If someone's not in a position to have a child—whether that's because the relationship isn't there, or the timing's wrong, or whatever the circumstances are—that's a pretty significant thing. I don't think someone should be forced into parenthood or marriage based on a pregnancy. That affects everything about her future.

I appreciate you asking, but I want to be honest here—this is one of those questions where I genuinely sit with tension on both sides.

I understand the argument about remedying past wrongs and ongoing inequities. I also understand concerns about fairness to individuals regardless of background. Both perspectives have real weight to me.

If I had to choose, I'd say **(C) not strongly opposes**, though it's closer to the middle than that framing suggests. I'm more persuaded by arguments about addressing systemic barriers than I am by concerns about individual reverse discrimination, but I don't feel strongly enough to pick a "strongly favors" option either.

The honest answer is I think the real question is more complicated than the binary presented—it's about *how* preferences are structured, what specific policies we're talking about, and whether they actually achieve their intended goals. That nuance doesn't fit cleanly into any single box.

But if forced to pick one answer: **(C)**.

I'd say **(E) about once a month**.

I'm not super regular about it, but I do make an effort to go when I can. Life gets busy, you know? But I think it's important to me to maintain that connection, so I try to get there at least monthly. Some months I make it more often, some months less—it really depends on what's going on.

I'd say **(B) inspired word** comes closest for me.

I think there's real spiritual truth and wisdom in the Bible, and I believe it was written by people genuinely trying to convey God's message. But I also recognize it was written by humans in specific historical contexts, so I don't think every single detail needs to be literal—especially when you've got different gospel accounts telling the same story slightly differently, or poetic passages that are clearly meant to be understood symbolically.

That middle ground feels most honest to how I actually think about it.

(B) oppose

Look, I understand why people support it—the severity of the crime, justice for victims' families, all that. But I've thought about this quite a bit, and I just can't get behind it. Too much risk of executing someone who's actually innocent, and once you do that, there's no taking it back. Plus, I'm not sure it actually deters murder the way people think it does. Life without parole seems like a reasonable alternative that doesn't require the state to take a life.

I'd say **(C) middle class**.

I've got a steady job, own my home, and can cover my bills and some extras without too much stress. But I'm not wealthy—I'm not living lavishly or anything. Most days feel pretty normal, you know? I work for what I have. That feels like the middle ground to me.

(A) yes, allowed to teach

Look, I think what matters for teaching at a college is whether someone knows their subject and can do the job well. Someone's personal beliefs about religion—whether they're deeply religious or completely against it—shouldn't disqualify them if they're a good educator.

I mean, colleges are supposed to be places where different ideas get debated and examined. A professor who's skeptical of religion could actually bring valuable perspective to discussions, especially in fields like philosophy, history, or literature where these questions come up.

The key would be that they teach their subject professionally and don't just use the classroom to push their personal views on students. But that's true for any professor, religious or not. If they can meet that standard, their personal stance on religion shouldn't matter.

I'd say **(B) only some confidence**.

Look, I respect what a lot of military personnel do and the job they're tasked with. But I have concerns about how leadership makes decisions, budget priorities, and accountability issues I've read about. It's not that I think they're all doing a bad job—it's more complicated than that. There are people in the military doing important work, but I can't say I have *great* confidence in the institution as a whole or the people running it.

I'd say **(B) only some** confidence.

Look, some companies do seem to have their act together and treat customers fairly, but there's always that underlying concern, you know? They're looking out for their bottom line first. You hear too many stories about corner-cutting, misleading advertising, or just not giving a damn about anything except profit. So I trust *some* of them in *some* ways, but I'm not naive about it. I keep my guard up.

I'd say **(B) only some**.

Look, I respect that religion is meaningful to a lot of people, and I appreciate the community and charitable work many religious institutions do. But I also see issues—misuse of funds, scandals, resistance to change on important issues. The people running these places are human, and some handle that responsibility better than others.

I'm not dismissive of faith itself, but when it comes to trusting the *institutions* and their leadership? I've got reservations. They need more accountability and transparency in my view.

I'd say **(B) only some** confidence.

Look, I think there are good people working in education who genuinely care about students. But there are real issues—overcrowding, funding problems, teaching to the test instead of actual learning. The leadership sometimes seems disconnected from what's actually happening in classrooms. I see both effort and shortcomings, so "only some" feels honest to me.

I'd say **(B) only some**.

Look, I think there are well-intentioned people in government trying to do their jobs, but there's also a lot of partisan gridlock and I don't always feel like my concerns are being heard at the top levels. Some policies make sense to me, others don't. It's hard to have complete confidence when things feel pretty divided and bureaucratic.

I'd say **(B) only some**.

Look, I need banks for basic stuff—checking accounts, loans if I need them. But after everything that's happened over the years, you can't help but be skeptical. There were the financial crises, the scandals, the fee structures that seem designed to nickel-and-dime you. I don't think they're all corrupt or anything, but I'm not under any illusions that they have my best interests at heart either.

They're businesses looking out for their bottom line. So yeah, "only some confidence" feels about right to me.

I'd say **(B) only some confidence**.

Look, I respect the institution and understand it plays an important role, but I've got concerns. Decisions seem increasingly divided along political lines, and I'm not always convinced the justices are above the political fray like they're supposed to be. They're making decisions that affect all of our lives, but there's not much accountability if I disagree with how they interpret things.

I don't think it's all broken—I don't have *hardly any* confidence. But *a great deal*? That feels too strong given what I see happening.

I'd say **(B) only some confidence**.

Look, I think unions have done important things historically—workplace safety, weekends, fair wages. That matters. But I'm realistic too. I've seen cases where unions seem more focused on protecting underperforming members than actually serving workers' interests well. And sometimes the leadership does seem out of touch with what regular members actually want.

So it's not that I have no confidence—organized labor still plays a role I think is needed. But I'm not starry-eyed about it either. There's room for improvement in how they operate.

I'd say **(B) only some** confidence.

Look, I think most members of Congress are trying to do their jobs, but there's a lot of gridlock and partisan bickering that makes it hard to get things done. They don't always seem to listen to regular people like me, and it feels like special interests have a lot of influence. That said, I'm not completely cynical about it—some representatives do seem genuine about helping their constituents. But overall? Yeah, just some confidence, not a lot.

I'd say **(B) only some confidence**.

Look, I think there are a lot of good doctors and researchers out there doing important work. But I've also seen enough—either personally or through people I know—to know the system isn't perfect. Sometimes it feels like it's more about profit than people. There are real issues with access, costs, and I've had experiences where I felt rushed or not fully listened to.

So yeah, I trust medicine itself as a science pretty well. But the institutions running it? They've got problems. I have confidence in the practice of medicine, but only *some* confidence in how it's actually being managed and delivered.

I'd say **(B) only some**.

Look, I think there are good journalists doing real work, but I've also seen enough corrections, retractions, and stories that feel slanted one way or another to know that confidence needs to be conditional. I try to read multiple sources and think critically about what I'm seeing. It's not that I think the press is entirely untrustworthy—that would be too extreme—but I'm not going to put blind faith in any single outlet or assume everything reported is completely accurate. Some skepticism just seems reasonable these days.

I'd say **(B) only some confidence**.

Look, I respect that scientists do important work, but I've noticed they don't always agree with each other, and sometimes what they say changes. Plus, you hear about studies that get retracted or don't hold up. I also think money and politics can influence what gets researched and published, which makes me a bit skeptical about taking everything at face value.

That said, I'm not dismissing them entirely—they know a lot more than I do about their fields. I just think it's smart to be somewhat cautious and not put blind faith in any institution.

I'd say **(B) only some confidence**.

Look, television news can be useful for getting information quickly, but I've noticed they don't always dig deep enough into stories, and sometimes the coverage feels sensationalized or leans a particular way depending on the network. The people running these institutions seem more focused on ratings and ad revenue than just giving you straight facts.

That said, I'm not saying I have *no* confidence—they do break important stories and employ real journalists. But I take what I see with a grain of salt and try to cross-check with other sources.

I'd say **(B) not harshly enough**.

Look, I see a lot of repeat offenders in the news around here, and it seems like people aren't facing real consequences. I get that the system is overcrowded and all that, but when you hear about someone with multiple arrests still on the streets, it's frustrating. It feels like there's not enough deterrent for people actually considering crime.

That said, I know I'm probably not seeing the whole picture—I don't follow every single case in detail. But based on what I hear and read, my sense is we could afford to be stricter.

I'd say **(C) stay as is**.

Look, I think the current process strikes a reasonable balance. Making it too easy might lead people to bail on marriages without really trying to work things out, especially when kids are involved. But making it harder seems like it would just trap people in situations that aren't working. 

The waiting periods and paperwork we have now give people time to be sure about their decision, which seems fair. If someone's made up their mind and gone through the process, they should be able to move on. I don't see a need to change it.

I'd say **(C) depends**.

Honestly, I think it really comes down to the person and the situation. Most people I interact with day-to-day seem decent—they want to be fair. But I'd be naive to think everyone operates that way, or that even good people won't cut corners if they feel justified or if the stakes are high enough.

I've seen both. I've had people go out of their way to be honest with me, and I've definitely had situations where someone took advantage when they thought they could get away with it. I guess I'm just realistic about human nature—most people lean toward fairness, but circumstances matter a lot.

*thinks for a moment*

I'd say **(B) agree**.

Look, I think what really matters is the quality of time and attention parents give their kids, not just the quantity of hours they're physically present. I've seen working mothers who are deeply connected to their children, and I've seen stay-at-home parents who struggle with that bond. It depends on the individual parent and how intentional they are about their relationship with their kids.

That said, I wouldn't go as far as "strongly agree" because I think it's not *always* equal—context matters. Work stress, childcare arrangements, and how present someone can be mentally all factor in. But the core idea? Yeah, working mothers can absolutely build that warm, secure relationship their kids need.

(D) strongly disagree

I think people should be able to choose their own paths regardless of gender. Some women want careers, some want to stay home—same with men. Forcing anyone into a role based on what they are rather than what they want just limits everyone's potential and happiness. Families work best when people do what actually works for *them*, not what tradition says they should do.

(B) disagree

I don't think gender determines emotional suitability for politics. I've seen plenty of men and women in politics—some handle pressure well, others don't. It comes down to individual temperament, experience, and training, not whether someone's a man or woman. That's just how I see it based on what I observe.

(C) disagree

Look, I think it really depends on the individual situation. A child's well-being comes down to the quality of care they receive, whether that's from their mother, a father, grandparent, or a good daycare center. I've seen kids thrive with working mothers and struggle with stay-at-home parents, and vice versa. What matters more is that the child is in a safe, nurturing environment and that parents are engaged and present when they're around. A mother working doesn't automatically harm a preschooler.

I'd say **(C) average**.

We do okay—nothing fancy, but we get by. My household income covers our expenses, allows for some savings, and we can afford occasional extras without constantly stressing about money. Not wealthy by any means, but we're comfortable. That feels pretty middle-of-the-road to me compared to what I know about other families around here.

(B) hard work, luck equally important

Look, I think both matter a lot. I've seen people work incredibly hard their whole lives and still struggle because circumstances weren't in their favor. And I've known people who got one good break that changed everything.

But I'd say hard work is probably the baseline—you need that to take advantage of luck when it comes. Without it, breaks don't lead anywhere. At the same time, I'm realistic enough to know that two equally hardworking people can end up in very different places depending on things outside their control—who they know, where they were born, timing of the economy, health stuff.

If I had to pick one as "most important," that's tough. But yeah, I'd say they're pretty equally important, and you need both.

I'd have to go with **(B) - don't know, no way to find out**.

Look, I respect people who have strong convictions either way, but I'm just being honest about where I'm at. I can't definitively say God doesn't exist, but I also don't have personal certainty that he does. And the more I think about it, the harder it seems to find a way to actually *know* for sure—it feels like something that's beyond what we can verify or disprove in any concrete way. So rather than pretend to a confidence I don't have, I sit with the uncertainty.
raw_responses.selected_option: don't know, no way to find out

I'd say **(A) should be legal**.

Look, I think prohibition hasn't really worked—we've seen that play out. People use it anyway, and making it illegal just creates problems: criminal markets, incarceration for nonviolent stuff, and people can't access it safely or know what they're getting.

If it's regulated and taxed like alcohol, the government can actually monitor quality, age restrictions work better, and we get tax revenue for schools or treatment programs. Plus, for medical use, there's real evidence it helps people with pain, nausea, and other conditions.

That said, I get why some people worry about impaired driving or youth access. Those are legitimate concerns that legalization would need to address properly. But overall, I think the harms of prohibition outweigh the harms of regulated legalization.

I'd say **(A) favor**.

Look, I think it makes sense to have some kind of screening process before someone buys a gun. A permit requirement would at least ensure that people have been checked out—background checks, maybe some basic safety training. It's similar to getting a driver's license before you can operate a car, right? 

I'm not trying to take anyone's guns away, but a permit system seems like a reasonable middle ground to keep firearms out of the hands of people who shouldn't have them while letting responsible people still own guns.

*pauses thoughtfully*

I'd say **(B) pretty happy**. 

Look, I can't complain too much. I've got what matters—decent health, people I care about, work that keeps me engaged. There are definitely things that frustrate me about the world and my own situation, but most days feel okay. Some days better than others, you know? I'm not walking around on cloud nine or anything, but I'm not struggling either. Pretty happy feels right—it's honest without being overly optimistic or pessimistic.

I'd say **(B) good**.

I don't have any major chronic conditions or anything that really limits me day-to-day. Sure, I get the occasional cold or back pain like everyone else, but overall I feel pretty solid. Not quite at "excellent" – I could probably exercise more and eat better – but definitely not struggling. Good feels right.

(C) depends

I'd say it really varies depending on the situation and who you're talking about. In my experience, most people have a mix of motivations. Like, someone might genuinely want to help a friend, but they're also thinking about their own time and energy. In professional settings, I've seen people be pretty self-interested, but then I've also witnessed real acts of kindness that cost people something.

I think context matters a lot too—whether someone's stressed, tired, or just going about their day affects how much they can afford to be generous. So yeah, I'd go with (C).

(D) not wrong at all

I think consenting adults should be free to make their own choices about their relationships. It's not my place to judge how other people live their lives, as long as everyone involved is a willing adult. What matters to me is that people treat each other with respect and honesty.

(C) don't know

I think this is one of those questions where reasonable people disagree, and I'm genuinely uncertain. There are real ethical tensions here—I understand the compassion behind wanting to end suffering, but I also see the risks around vulnerable people feeling pressured, or mistakes being made.

I'd want to know more specifics: What safeguards would be in place? How do we ensure it's truly voluntary? What about palliative care options? These details matter a lot to me before I could give a firmer answer.

It's not that I'm dodging it—I just think this deserves more thought than a simple yes or no from me.

(B) not remove

Look, I may not agree with everything someone writes, but that doesn't mean it shouldn't be in the library. A public library should have different viewpoints—including ones that challenge religion if that's what the author believes. 

If we start removing books just because they go against what some community members believe in, where does it stop? Today it's a book critical of churches, tomorrow it could be something else. People need access to different ideas to make up their own minds.

I'd rather have the book there and let people decide for themselves whether to read it or not.

I'd say **(B) routine**.

Don't get me wrong—there are definitely exciting moments, you know? But honestly, most days follow a pretty predictable pattern. Work, home, the usual stuff. I think that's probably true for most people. It's not dull exactly, because I've got things I care about and people I enjoy spending time with. But I wouldn't describe my everyday life as exciting either. It's steady. Comfortable, mostly. That works for me.

(C) too much

Look, I understand we have real problems here at home—infrastructure that needs fixing, healthcare costs people can't afford, schools that need better funding. When I think about foreign aid, it just feels like we're stretching ourselves too thin. We're sending money overseas while we've got people struggling right here.

I'm not saying we shouldn't help other countries at all, but when budgets are tight everywhere, it seems like the priority should be taking care of our own people first. That's just how I see it.

I'd say **(C) too much**.

Look, I understand we need a strong defense, but when I look at the numbers—we're spending more on military than the next several countries combined. Meanwhile, there are real problems at home: healthcare costs, infrastructure falling apart, education funding. 

It feels like we've got our priorities backwards. We could maintain national security with less and redirect some of those resources to things that actually affect my daily life and my family's wellbeing. Defense contractors aren't exactly hurting for money, either.

That said, I'm not naive about the world being dangerous. But "right amount" shouldn't mean "whatever we're currently spending." There's definitely room to cut without compromising security.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, I see the problems in cities every time I drive through or visit—crumbling infrastructure, homelessness, struggling schools. These aren't things you can fix with pocket change. And honestly, when you break down where government money actually goes, cities often get squeezed between competing priorities. 

You need real investment to make a dent in housing, transportation, education—not just band-aids. So yeah, we're underfunding the real solutions, even though I understand the budget concerns. It costs money to fix these things properly.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, crime affects everyone—neighborhoods, schools, property values. You see the news about what's happening in a lot of cities. It seems like we're not investing enough in the things that actually work: more police presence, community programs, mental health services, job training. 

A lot of what we *do* spend just goes to locking people up after the fact, which doesn't solve the root problems. We need more prevention and intervention, which takes real money. So yeah, I think we're underfunded in this area.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, drug addiction is everywhere—it's affecting families, communities, workplaces. We see the opioid crisis, homelessness tied to substance abuse, people cycling through the criminal justice system instead of getting treatment. 

From what I can tell, treatment programs have waiting lists, not enough prevention education reaches people early enough, and there's still a lot of stigma keeping people from seeking help. If we're serious about addressing this problem, we need more funding for treatment, better access to medication-assisted therapy, more counselors and support services.

It costs money upfront, yeah, but untreated addiction costs us way more in emergency room visits, lost productivity, crime, and broken families. So to me, we're investing too little right now.

I'd have to say **(A) too little**.

Look, I know money isn't everything when it comes to education—good teachers, engaged families, solid curriculum all matter. But the reality is that schools in a lot of areas are struggling with basic things: outdated facilities, overcrowded classrooms, teachers buying supplies out of pocket. 

When I think about what we're competing with globally, and the investment we'd need to really overhaul things—better teacher pay to attract talent, modernized infrastructure, more support for struggling students—it seems like we're consistently underfunding what we say is a priority.

That said, I understand the concern about waste and efficiency too. But my gut sense is we're cutting corners in a way that'll cost us more down the road.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, I know everything costs money and we've got competing priorities everywhere. But when I think about what's actually happening—the air quality issues, the water problems, extreme weather getting worse—it seems like we're not doing enough to address it. And the costs of *not* acting tend to pile up later in bigger ways.

That said, I get that people have different views on this depending on where they live and what they've experienced. But from my perspective, environmental protection isn't getting the resources it needs.

I'd say **(C) too much**.

Look, I understand people need help, and there are folks genuinely struggling. But from what I see, a lot of welfare money gets lost to bureaucracy and doesn't reach the people who actually need it most. Plus, some people are taking advantage of the system when they could be working. 

We're already spending a huge amount on it, and I'm not convinced throwing more money at it will fix anything without serious reforms first. So yeah, too much in my view—at least the way it's currently set up.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, healthcare costs keep going up, but a lot of people still can't afford decent care or preventive services. You see stories about people rationing medications or skipping doctor visits because of costs. And we're dealing with aging populations, chronic diseases, mental health issues that aren't getting enough attention. 

Yeah, we're spending a lot in absolute dollars, but it doesn't feel like it's reaching the people who need it most. A lot of that money goes to administrative overhead and profits rather than actual care. So while the total spending is high, I think we need to be spending *smarter* and probably *more* on the actual health side of things—prevention, mental health, rural healthcare access.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, there are real disparities out there—in education funding, healthcare access, housing, criminal justice. Whether you're talking about predominantly Black neighborhoods getting less school funding or health outcomes being worse in certain communities, the data shows gaps. If we're serious about addressing those problems, you have to invest resources proportionally to need.

That said, I think a lot of people across the spectrum could probably agree the money that *is* being spent should be better managed and more effective. But the overall level of investment? Not enough relative to the scale of the problems.

I'd have to go with **(C) too much**.

Look, I get that space exploration is interesting and important for science and technology. But when you've got so many pressing problems here at home—crumbling infrastructure, healthcare costs, education funding—it's hard to justify spending billions on space programs. 

Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying cut it entirely. But we could probably do more good directing those resources toward things that directly help people struggling right now. It feels like a luxury we can't quite afford when there's so much else that needs fixing first.

(B) no

I don't own any firearms. Never really felt the need for one, and honestly, the safety considerations involved just weren't worth it for me personally.

I'd say **(D) independent (neither, no response)**.

I try not to lock myself into one party. I look at issues individually and don't feel like either major party really represents everything I care about. Some years I lean one way on certain things, other years it's different. I just don't feel strongly enough about the party label itself to pick one.

I'd say **(D) moderate, middle of the road**.

I don't feel like I fit neatly into either camp. I've got views that lean different directions depending on the issue—some positions feel more progressive to me, others more traditional. On most things, I'm somewhere in the center trying to weigh different perspectives rather than holding strong ideological commitments across the board.

I'd go with **(B) there should be laws against the distribution of pornography to persons under 18**.

That feels like the reasonable middle ground to me. I think protecting kids from that stuff makes sense—their brains are still developing, you know? But I'm not comfortable saying all adults should be banned from accessing it. That feels like overreach into personal freedom.

Option A seems too restrictive for adults, and option C doesn't account for protecting minors. So B is where I land.
raw_responses.selected_option: there should be laws against the distribution of pornography to persons under 18

raw_responses.raw_text:
(C) don't know

Honestly, I think that's the most truthful answer for me. I don't have any way to really know what happens after we die. I've heard arguments on both sides—spiritual beliefs, scientific perspectives, personal experiences people share—but none of it feels like certain knowledge to me.

I guess I lean toward thinking there's *something* rather than complete nothingness, just based on how vast and mysterious the universe seems. But whether that's actually "life" in any meaningful sense? I really can't say. It's one of those big questions I've kind of made peace with not having a definitive answer to.

(A) approve

I think that's the right call. Public schools serve students from all kinds of backgrounds and beliefs—Christian, Jewish, Muslim, atheist, you name it. A public school shouldn't be pushing any particular religious practice on kids, even something as traditional as the Lord's Prayer.

If parents want their kids learning religious material, that's something they can do at home, church, or a private school. But in a public school that taxpayers fund regardless of their beliefs, I think it makes sense to keep it neutral on religion.

I'd say **(D) not wrong at all**.

Look, people are adults who can make their own choices about their relationships. What matters to me is that there's mutual respect, honesty, and consent between them. Whether they're married or not doesn't really change that for me.

I think a lot of people today see it differently than previous generations did, and I'm comfortable with that perspective.

I'd vote for the second law (B).

Look, I think people should have basic protections against discrimination when they're trying to buy a home. Housing is fundamental—it's not like choosing who to invite to a dinner party. If we let discrimination happen in housing, whole groups of people get locked out of building wealth and stability.

The first law basically legalizes racial discrimination, and I don't think that's right. History shows us what happens when that's allowed—segregation, inequality, blocked opportunities.

That said, I recognize this touches on property rights, which people care about. But I think the civil right to equal access to housing outweighs that concern here.

I'd say **(B) more or less satisfied**.

Look, we're getting by okay. Bills are paid, we have what we need, but there's always that underlying stress, you know? Groceries cost more than they used to, and I worry about unexpected expenses popping up. We're not struggling desperately, but we're not comfortable enough to stop thinking about money either. It's that middle ground where you're managing but not thriving.

I'd say **(A) favor**, though I think it matters how it's done.

Kids are going to learn about sex one way or another—better they get accurate, age-appropriate information from educators than just figure it out from peers or the internet. It should cover basics like anatomy, consent, STI prevention, and healthy relationships.

That said, I get that people have different values and beliefs about this stuff. I just think opting out of education doesn't solve anything—it just leaves gaps that get filled with misinformation.

I'd say **(C) disagree**.

Look, I get that parenting is hard and frustration happens. But I think there are better ways to handle discipline that actually teach kids something. Spanking might stop behavior in the moment, but it doesn't help them understand *why* they shouldn't do something. And honestly, it can escalate things—model aggression as a way to solve problems, you know?

I'm not saying parents are bad for using it, but I don't think it's *necessary*. Timeout, taking away privileges, clear consequences that make sense—those seem more effective in the long run.

I'd say **(A) yes, allowed to speak**.

Look, I might disagree with someone's views on religion—a lot of people in my community would—but that doesn't mean they shouldn't be allowed to say them. Free speech is important. People need to be able to express unpopular opinions, even ones I find offensive or misguided.

Besides, if we start saying certain viewpoints can't be expressed, where does that end? It gets messy fast. Better to let people speak and let the community respond, debate, or ignore them as they see fit.

I'd go with **(A) yes, allowed to speak**.

Look, I don't agree with communist ideology—that's not really my thing. But if we're talking about what *should* be allowed in a free society, I think people need the right to express unpopular views, even ones I strongly disagree with. 

The way I see it, if we start saying "this group of people can't speak because we don't like what they believe," where does that stop? It's a slippery slope. Better to let people hear different ideas and make up their own minds about them.

Plus, someone giving a speech isn't the same as them actually implementing policies or anything. It's just words. I can handle hearing someone I disagree with speak and still be fine.

I'd choose **(A) yes, allowed to speak**.

Look, I think that view is repugnant and scientifically baseless. But I'm troubled by the idea of the government or community authorities deciding what speech is acceptable. That power gets misused.

The better response is that yes, he can speak—but he'll face pushback, criticism, and social consequences. People should counter his claims, not silence him. That's how bad ideas actually get defeated in the open rather than festering underground.

If there are specific threats or incitement to violence, that's different. But just expressing a racist belief, however wrong? I lean toward allowing it while firmly opposing it.

I'd say **(C) don't know**.

Look, it's a genuinely difficult question. I can see arguments both ways. On one hand, if someone's in unbearable pain from an incurable disease, I understand the compassion behind saying they should have that choice—that it's about personal autonomy and dignity.

But on the other hand, there are real concerns—about whether people are truly making free choices when they're depressed or in crisis, about protecting vulnerable people, about the role of medicine and palliative care. And there are deep personal and religious beliefs involved.

I don't think there's a clear-cut answer that works for everyone. It depends on the specifics—the person's situation, their mental state, what medical options exist. It's something that needs really careful, individual consideration, probably with doctors, counselors, family involved.

So yeah, I honestly don't know. I lean toward thinking compassion matters here, but I can't give you a simple yes or no.

*pauses thoughtfully*

I'd say **(A) too high**.

Look, I understand the government needs revenue for roads, schools, and all that. But when I see how much gets taken out of each paycheck, combined with state taxes and everything else, it feels like a significant chunk. And then you hear about how some of it gets spent... I'm not always confident I'm getting good value for what I'm paying in.

That said, I know reasonable people disagree on this one. But yeah, if I'm being honest, I think it's too much.

I'd say **(C) depends**.

Look, I think most people in my everyday life—neighbors, coworkers, people at the store—are generally honest and mean well. But I've also learned that trust needs to be earned, especially with bigger things. 

It depends on the situation and who you're dealing with. I trust my family completely. I'm cautious with strangers, especially if money's involved. And with institutions or businesses, I've learned you do need to be careful—read the fine print, don't just take things at face value.

So it's not black and white for me. I'm optimistic about people, but I'm not naive either.

I'd say **(D) disagree somewhat**.

Look, I understand the appeal of that argument—there's something to the idea that many groups faced real discrimination and still made progress. But the statement glosses over some important differences.

Those other groups faced serious prejudice, sure, but they could eventually assimilate—they became "white" over time in a way that Black Americans couldn't, no matter what. Plus, slavery and Jim Crow weren't just prejudice; they were systematic legal exclusion from wealth-building for centuries. Redlining kept Black families out of neighborhoods where white families built generational wealth through home ownership. That's not the same as what Irish or Italian immigrants faced.

So when the statement compares them as if the situations were equivalent, I have to push back a bit. The barriers aren't identical, so expecting identical outcomes without acknowledging those differences doesn't quite add up to me.

That said, I get why some people see it that way—there's a reasonable concern about fairness and self-reliance embedded in the question. But I can't fully agree with it.

I'd say **(B) almost always wrong**.

Look, I think marriage comes with a commitment, and infidelity breaks that trust in a pretty fundamental way. For most situations, that's clearly a betrayal.

But I'm hesitant to say "always" because I can imagine edge cases—like maybe a couple has an explicit agreement about an open marriage, or there are circumstances I haven't thought through. So "almost always" feels more honest to me than absolute.

In the vast majority of cases though, it's wrong. It violates the terms of the relationship and hurts the other person.
